title: OpenAI’s Sora could kill commercial film – good riddance?

commenti.body:
There are strong major hurdles to figure out prior to this being able to use to create a movie. Right now, they can make 1 minute movies. They can’t create 2 hour movies. That will probably be solved over time…. 

Another major issue though, is it can’t iterate, or control details. I don’t think that’s getting solved anytime doom. If you say show me a dog, in a home, eating dog food. You’ll get a video. If your next statement is change the dog to a cat. You’ll get a completely different video, different house, different wherever.  You can’t control what stays and what goes.
[removed]

Those things are already been worked on. A designer friend of mine showed me an AI platform a month or two ago that iterated still images exactly how you wanted. All you had to do is reload the previous image, and could even point to and highlight the details you wanted to change or replace. This kind of feature will likely come to video before the year is even over.

The rate of innovation and change is unprecedented. At the very least, it puts the entire VFX industry on notice because a lot of big VFX-only wide shots in blockbuster films will be easily created with AI in a fraction of the time it normally takes to design and animate them.

>If you say show me a dog, in a home, eating dog food. You’ll get a video. If your next statement is change the dog to a cat. You’ll get a completely different video, different house, different wherever.  You can’t control what stays and what goes.

Very true. I think there will probably be some curious ways it can be used once it gets more advanced. Like could even the randomness of generative AI somehow be harnessed into something that feels born from human creativity? Time will tell, though the way major studios will use it might make it a pariah for filmmakers. I guess it's important to assess every possibility even tho on the surface AI and its effect will make it a natural enemy.
[removed]

> Like could even the randomness of generative AI somehow be harnessed into something that feels born from human creativity?

Whether it's liked or not the answer is a resounding yes. Same with rock to paper to canvas to photo to silent pictures to talkies to color to digital to cgi. If change doesn't happen through AI it will happen in some other form. So let's say AI doesn't take off, well something else will.

> AI and its effect will make it a natural enemy

also to note is other countries with laxer restrictions that won't be shy implementing the tech. Actually, a lot of the services we use today is through auto stats, including advertisement.

And calling it "AI" isn't even a correct term. It's just more sophisticated statistical aggregation.
[removed]

As a filmmaker, I can see using it for matte pantings, set extensions, things like that. But having played with similar tools, it's just not built for scene work, for hero shots.   
We've seen the astronaut footage. It looks good in 1 second clips.  
But if you tell it to change the lighting, it's gotta rebuild the whole thing from scratch and you'll get a whole new astronaut with a slightly different face and similar but different helmet, suit etc. That's *IF* it gives you the lighting you want. Now, tell it to correct the performance of the actor, to make it walk different. These tools are not built for the kind of granular control that filmmakers need.

I'll be honest I find it really hard to believe this will replace commercial filmmaking. Have other AI generators replaced writers and voice actors? And making a movie is far more complicated and difficult than just writing an article or recording/creating a voice.  But these machines are more like spam creators than anything.  


But eh, maybe I'm wrong, I just don't think it'll kill the film industry be anytime soon. Movies are still going to be made by big studios, this just might streamline the movie making process in the short term.
[removed]

Not really because independent and arthouse films are way more heterodox than mainstream films; as in non-traditional, lo-fi storytelling with non-algorithmic, non cookie-cutter plot points.  There's enough big-budget franchise films where this isn't so much the case, which could more reasonably inject more AI into their filmmaking processes.
[removed]

I think someone could make a very interesting “waking life” style movie with a technology like this in a few years or like a very trippy AI version of koyaanisqatsi or even churn out some interesting footage for history documentaries.

Ive already seen some interesting video art made from AI video.

But its hard to know what will be possible in 20 years.

I think the first concern with come with Advertising jobs drying first, a quick google search showed Coca-Cola spent $645.4 million on advertising in 2022 >!https://digiday.com/marketing/coca-cola-believes-in-music-in-ads-so-much-it-is-growing-its-own-studio-to-record-original-songs/#:\~:text=During%20the%20first%20quarter%20of,and%20%24602.4%20million%20in%202021.!<  


with a Sora-style generative AI Coke could potentially make 100s of ads a week that a much smaller team can control, but this would put a lot of creatives out of steady work in a current market that is already pretty scary for a lot of those jobs.
[removed]

Not good riddance 

If you remove professional positions in the arts, the only people making professional films will be people so rich they didn't need to get a real job. 

Obviously they can't fully replace everything overnight, but we should want a Hollywood that provides tons of jobs at all levels, across all all departments.

I’ll put it this way. Right now the AI age industry is mostly aiming to disrupt the stock footage industry. The training dataset for Sora seems to be mostly just that, stock footage. The whole goal of the generative AI industry, for all its partisans bluster about creativity being unleashed for the masses, is to be a cheapening aid for white collar corporate work. Get art and text for your powerpoint without the work or the labor, that kind of thing.

Sora, right now, can generate single shots from a text prompt. It’s public-facing application has very little ability to control of shape exact technical shot requirements. It seems to be great for these epic looking showoff pieces, but I suspect it will struggle if you ask it to generate a conversation between two people in a grocery store. It’s still fundamentally a learning model, it isn’t sentient, and it can only pretend to remember things.

Let’s go back to that grocery store example, and let’s pretend it’s six months in the future and the technology is super duper improved, to the point where its a legitimate threat. You are an AI filmmaker. The client needs a master and two over the shoulder shots of Timothee Chalamet and Sir Alec Guinness discussing the product in the dairy aisle. It’s been trained on data of all that information. The client needs aHow do you get it 100% accurate?

Do you ask it to generate the whole sequence? How do you stop it from hallucinating and going offscript and off-model? It doesn’t understand your instructions and won’t give you a coherent sequence. Okay, so we program in each shot at a time. Wonderful. How do we keep every element in the shot consistent? The shelves keep changing design. It’s decided this shot is 35mm and we want 50mm. Guinness’s suit keep changing. It keep generating extras with gigantic breasts because the people who design these training models are horny weebs, so we have to throw in more keywords in order to negate that out, but it keeps fucking up other elements in the scene. And the lipsync is fucked even still, subtly off, so we can’t integrate it with the voice-generated audio, which we had trouble doing anyway because ElevenLabs and OpenAI have shut down. Why didn’t we just shoot in a real supermarket, or even on the Volume, with stand-ins? 

The technology will jump in leaps and bounds, because that’s the nature of both computing and everyone’s damned enthusiasm for improving these fucking things, but for the purposes of even a simple commercial, it’s still going to be a headache. One that a lot of greedy execs will regret embracing. It isn’t designed to disrupt commercial filmmaking. It’s designed as a toy for drones to grab stock footage.
Generating video is a bit much at this point. But commercial scripts? Those can be automated *easily*, pretty much commercials are already fucking trash so there's no way they'd be worse

> Like could even the randomness of generative AI somehow be harnessed into something that feels born from human creativity? 

Conceptual artists have been doing similar things with similar programs for almost three decades now. That is nothing new at all and probably a more artistically valid and correct way to use such a technology than a bunch of techbros drooling that they can take filmmaking away from those dumb fucking artists and make what *they* wanna see.

If you’re freaking out about this, you don’t fundamentally understand it and you’re panicking because a street magician said a magic box could replace your job. The entire AI industry is smoke and mirrors. Their programs are much more limited than they boast about and promise, even if they “get better and better.” Today a single number in ChatGPT’s code was off and it spouted nonsense Spanglish all day. They will be a nuisance to integrate into daily life.

You’re not wrong. At least for a while. There’s not any way to edit anything. To tweak. Film and art and storytelling is iterative. 

This just spits out a bunch of video vomit.
[removed]

you’re right about this, particularly when it comes to voice.

I had a client get pretty excited about an AI voiceover tool he found, and I was pretty excited too, since finding VO artists generally isn’t my favorite part of the job (I’m primarily an animator). after hearing two takes we binned it and just went forward with no VO at all - the voice sounded _okay_, but the intonation was terrible.

I mean with voice acting I am starting to see instances where it’s being replaced (like I think some mods for games used it). Considering that it’s been only around a year since realistic voice ai really became a thing, I’d say that things will look a lot different in 5 years.
[removed]
You’ll be surprised how much can be done with clever editing.. I can totally see a scenario where 70% of the shots are AI especially the wide shots

James Cameron is a fanatic who has been on Team CGI since near enough day 1. He has also never been told no once in his entire life.

Avatar: Way Of The Water took WETA 3 years, 1,700 animators and so much computing they had to hire out full farms. All told, Cameron spent around $350m, and still did a lot of it through mocap to make it look right.

But sure. AI has made that obsolete 2 years later, and this definitely isn’t a hype train for an obvious grift.

I believe that some protectionist legislation will be passed for the creative industries (and others, but that's besides the scope of this sub) before Sora or other AI's advance to that point. Also, this assumes that the costs to use them will be lower than the use of a regular production team. The company that will license it would probably price it similarly.
My wife works for a large casting company. AI voice is already being used frequently for radio ads. It’s coming for more and more jobs, absolutely.

Give it 3 years.  Honestly.  All kids shows could be made with these ai tools.


I think this thread is seriously under selling how big of a game changer this is.  Especially for small networks.
